This New Loan Is Bringing Investors to Abandoned Towns
 
Plus, the developer of a $10 billion real-estate project is asking its condo buyers for money
 
By Craig Karmin
 

This is an edition of the Real Estate newsletter, a weekly briefing of the biggest commercial deals, news, analysis and trends in office, multifamily, retail and other commercial sectors. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

Places like East Cleveland, Ohio, aren’t used to getting real-estate investment. The federal government once warned banks that lending there was risky. But a new kind of mortgage is flooding the area, helping real-estate investors buy, renovate and rent out vacant and dilapidated homes. The approval process for a traditional mortgage evaluates how likely the borrower is to pay back the loan. In the new model, a private lender approves the loan based on the property’s value and potential rental income. These loans have helped revitalize neighborhoods in Indianapolis, Baltimore, and Memphis. As Nicholas G. Miller reports, the loans have also been susceptible to fraud.

 

The developer behind one of the country’s most expensive real-estate projects has an unusual request for its condo buyers: Lend us money. Purchasers of the site’s 150 condo units are also providing debt to help Cain, an investment firm based in London, fund its $10 billion project, known as One Beverly Hills. The condo owners’ debt takes the form of a bond—the developers call them Founder Bonds—and buyers will receive a return of 5%. Nicholas explains how it works and how many of these Founder Bonds have been sold.

 
 
 

A New Type of Mortgage Is Reviving Long Abandoned Neighborhoods

 
 
TRAVARRIS LEAKS
 

A new loan product, together with the increasing lure of cheap neighborhoods as housing costs have risen sharply elsewhere, has helped inject capital across American cities that could use the boost, including Indianapolis, Baltimore, Detroit and Memphis.

 

The new mortgages, launched in the mid-2010s and called debt-service coverage ratio loans, are part of a private lending industry that has exploded, drawing borrowers with its flexible underwriting, simplicity and speed.

Celebrate the Season at Level Ten
 
Make it a night to remember at Level Ten, located at The Starrett-Lehigh Building. Bring your team together in versatile multipurpose event spaces, customized for your event and designed for gathering. Enjoy hand-crafted canapés, attended buffet receptions, and cocktail party service, with every detail thoughtfully considered. Reserve before 10/31 for exclusive enhancements.
 
Learn More  >
 
 
 

The Luxury Beverly Hills Condo Project Borrowing Money From Its Future Residents

 
 
FOSTER & PARTNERS
 

Buyers of the roughly 150 condo units at the $10 billion development called One Beverly Hills are providing debt to help the project’s developer, Cain, an investment firm based in London.

 

No condo buyers are forced to participate in the bond program. Some say this rarely seen financing tool sticks condo buyers with a risk. If the condo towers were to fall short of completion—in a city where most luxury buyers are focused on single-family homes and estates—bondholders could be left not only without the penthouse they were expecting, but also without the extra money lent to the developers.

 
 
 
$1 Billion
 

The value of condos that are already under contract or reserved at One Beverly Hills.

 
 
 

How 7.4% Mortgages Are Giving Buyers Leverage in a Stuck Housing Market

 
 
TRAVIS DOVE/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Mortgage rates hitting their highest point in nearly three years is lousy news for an overall stagnant housing market, but the upward pressure on borrowing costs is starting to force some sellers to cut prices, offering buyers a glimmer of relief. The housing market is “leaning a little bit more towards a buyer market right now,” said Kathryn McNeill, an agent in North Carolina.

 
 
 

Data Points

 

• 572,000: The square feet of office space that AI companies leased in New York in the third quarter, a 16% increase from the previous quarter, according to CoStar.

 

• 4.5%: The annual decline of housing affordability in the Northeast in September, the sharpest drop of any other region, according to the National Association of Realtors.
